author: 内置生成器草稿

paragraphs.text: Last September, our school started a Reading Club to help students enjoy books. It meets every Tuesday afternoon in the school library for about an hour. Members choose a book together, read it at home, and then meet to share their ideas.

At first, only eight students joined. The club adviser, Miss Yang, invited some senior students to recommend their favourite books at the school gate. Soon more students became interested, and now the club has over forty members. 'I used to think reading was boring,' says Lin Tao, a club member. 'But when I talk about a story with others, I find more fun in it.' This term, the club plans to invite a local writer to talk about how stories are created.

Have you ever seen a fox in a city? In London, foxes are now a common sight. At night, they search dustbins for food and sleep in quiet gardens during the day. Scientists say that city foxes are smaller and braver than wild ones.

Why have so many foxes moved into cities? The main reason is easy food. People throw away a lot of food every day, and foxes quickly learn where to find it. Also, cities are warmer than the countryside in winter, which helps foxes survive the cold. Some people enjoy watching these clever animals, while others complain that foxes make their gardens dirty. Experts advise people not to feed foxes, because food from humans makes them lose their fear and cause more trouble.

Every Saturday morning, Maria, a sixteen-year-old student, teaches swimming to children in her neighbourhood for free. She began the class two years ago after she read about a child who nearly drowned in a local river.

At first, only three children came, and some parents worried that a teenager was too young to teach. Maria showed them her lifeguard certificate and invited the parents to watch her lessons by the pool. Now more than twenty children have learned basic swimming skills safely with her help. 'The best moment is when a child swims across the pool for the first time,' Maria says. She plans to train other teenagers as helpers so that the free class can continue even after she goes to university.

At No. 5 Middle School, students in Grade One run for twenty minutes every morning before the first class. The school started the activity three years ago, and many students say it has changed their school life.

'I often felt sleepy in class before,' says Wang Bo, a Grade One student. 'Now running wakes my body up, and I can listen to the teachers better.' Doctors agree that morning exercise improves blood flow to the brain and helps young people sleep at night. However, they also warn that students should not run too fast at the beginning, or their knees may get hurt. Warming up for five minutes and drinking some water after the run are simple but useful rules. The school plans to add a health record for each student to show how daily exercise works.

Twelve-year-old Kate hates forgetting things, so she invented a 'talking umbrella'. A small chip inside the handle connects to her phone. When she walks more than fifty metres away from the umbrella, the phone gives a warning sound.

Kate got the idea after she lost three umbrellas in one rainy season. She spent two months learning basic electronics online and built her first model with parts from an old radio. Her invention won first prize at a city science fair, and a company now wants to produce the umbrella. 'Science is not only for adults in labs,' Kate says. 'If you keep asking why, ideas will come to you.' She is now working on a schoolbag that can remind students to take their homework.

Every day, people around the world throw away billions of paper coffee cups. Most cups are lined with a thin plastic film, so they cannot be recycled like ordinary paper. They end up in landfills and stay there for many years, polluting the soil.

A cafe owner named Mr. Lee decided to fight this problem. He offers customers a small discount if they bring their own cups. He also places bright green collection boxes outside his cafe, and a factory turns the collected cups into flower pots and park benches. In one year, his cafe has collected more than eighty thousand cups. 'Change starts with small steps,' Mr. Lee says. Now several other cafes in the city are copying his idea.

Shadow puppetry, an art with a history of over two thousand years, was once one of the most popular forms of entertainment in China. In the past, travelling performers set up a white cloth screen in village squares after dark. Behind the screen, they moved flat leather figures and sang stories of heroes, ghosts and happy families, while villagers sat around and watched the shadows dance in the lamplight.

Making a single puppet can take a skilled artist several weeks. The leather must be cleaned, carved with fine patterns and painted in bright colours. A good performer also needs years of practice, because each puppet has three sticks, and the hands must move together smoothly to make the figures walk, fight or fly.

Today, however, fewer and fewer young people are willing to learn this slow art, and many famous troupes have closed. To keep it alive, some artists now perform in schools and teach students simple cutting skills. Others put their shows online, where short videos have attracted millions of viewers. 'The shadows are old, but the stage can be new,' one artist says. With fresh ideas and patient hands, this ancient art may continue to light up the dark.

Many students believe that reading a text again and again is the best way to learn it. However, a number of studies in psychology suggest a different method: testing yourself. In one famous experiment, two groups of students studied the same passage. One group read it four times, while the other group read it once and then spent the rest of the time answering questions about it. A week later, the second group remembered much more.

Why does testing work so well? Scientists explain that when the brain tries to pull information out, it builds a stronger path to that information, which makes it easier to find later. Rereading, on the other hand, often gives students a false feeling of mastery: the words look familiar, so they believe they have learned them, but familiarity is not real memory.

Teachers now suggest some simple ways to use this method. After finishing a chapter, close the book and write down everything you remember; then check what you missed. You can also explain the lesson to a friend in your own words, or make flashcards and review them over several days instead of cramming all at once. Testing yourself may feel harder than rereading, but that difficulty is exactly what makes the memory last.

In some mountain villages, a visit to the nearest hospital can take hours on winding roads. For patients who need urgent medicine, every minute matters. In recent years, drone delivery has become a surprising answer to this problem. Medical drones fly above the mountains, carrying blood, vaccines and other supplies in small boxes. Guided by satellite navigation, they can reach a village clinic in twenty minutes, a journey that once took two hours by car.

The technology is already changing lives. In one African country, thousands of emergency deliveries are made every month, and the time needed to send blood to hospitals has dropped greatly. Nurses simply send a text message, and the drone sets off within minutes. Local health workers say that mothers giving birth and children with malaria have been the groups helped most.

Still, drone delivery faces challenges. Drones cannot fly in strong winds or heavy rain, and each flight needs trained operators on the ground. Some people also worry about the noise and the safety of low-flying machines. Governments are now writing rules to balance these concerns. Most experts, however, believe the future is clear: as the technology becomes cheaper and safer, drones will quietly become a normal part of health care, bringing help to places that roads cannot easily reach.

As a child, Chen Jin had to cross a shaky wooden bridge on her way to school. On rainy days, the river below rose, and the bridge swayed so much that the children held hands and walked across one by one. 'One day I will build a bridge here,' she told her classmates. Few of them took her words seriously.

Years later, Chen became a bridge engineer. In 2018, she returned to her hometown as the chief designer of a new river bridge. The project was far from easy. The valley's strong winds and sudden floods forced her team to change their design three times. During the hardest months, she lived in a tent near the site and checked every calculation herself. When the bridge finally opened, the schoolchildren crossed it in two minutes on their way to class.

Chen often tells this story at universities. 'A bridge is not just steel and concrete,' she says. 'It is a promise made to a child.' Today, she leads a programme that invites engineering students to build small footbridges in remote villages. For her, every new bridge is a chance to keep an old promise.

Sunlight can only reach the top two hundred metres of the ocean. Below that lies the deep sea, a world of darkness, crushing pressure and near-freezing water. For a long time, scientists believed that nothing could live there. Then, in 1977, a research ship sent a small vessel down to the ocean floor near hot springs, and the cameras showed something amazing: whole communities of creatures living around the springs, including giant tube worms as long as a person.

These creatures do not need sunlight at all. Tiny bacteria inside them turn the chemicals from the springs into food, and larger animals feed on the bacteria. Scientists call this a food chain based on chemicals instead of light. The discovery changed how we think about life. If life can exist in such an extreme place on Earth, it may also exist under the ice of distant moons like Europa.

The deep sea remains one of the least explored places on our planet. Many of its creatures have never been named, and some may hold chemicals useful for new medicines. Sadly, deep-sea mining and plastic pollution are already threatening this fragile world. Scientists warn that we should understand the deep sea before we damage it, because once these slow-growing communities are destroyed, they may need centuries to recover.

In many old neighbourhoods, empty corners once served as rubbish dumps. Today, more and more of them are turning green. Residents are turning these small spaces into community gardens, where families can grow vegetables and flowers together. The idea started in big cities where people live in tall buildings without yards of their own, and it has quickly spread to smaller towns.

A community garden does more than provide fresh tomatoes. Gardeners meet almost every day, and neighbours who never said hello before now share seeds, tools and recipes. Older residents teach younger ones how to keep insects away without chemicals, and children learn where their food really comes from. In one garden in Chengdu, a wall was built where residents hang small bags of vegetables for anyone who needs them.

City governments have noticed the change. Some now offer free soil, water pipes and gardening classes to new gardens. Researchers have also found that people who garden report lower stress and get to know more neighbours. Of course, gardens need patient work: weeds grow fast, and summer heat tests everyone's energy. But as one gardener put it, 'We came for the vegetables, but we stayed for the people.'
